query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy bond coats with Yttrium (Y) and Hafnium (Hf) improves coating durability and reliability for high-temperature applications by enhancing oxidation resistance and stabilizing the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy bond coats without rare earth element doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled co-doping of Y and Hf into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy during the bond coat preparation process (e.g., via laser cladding).
generation.conditions: Exposure at high temperatures (around 900 °C) in corrosive molten salt environments (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl by weight), simulating operational conditions in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified microstructure with enhanced phase stability, where Y and Hf promote the formation of a more adherent and protective oxide scale while reducing interfacial energy and diffusion rates across phases.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf co-doping encourages the formation of a stable, resilient oxide layer that limits further oxidation and hot corrosion. These elements also reduce rapid atomic diffusion at high temperature, thereby maintaining the integrity of the eutectic microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Co-doped bond coats will exhibit lower oxidation and corrosion rates, improved retention of mechanical properties, and greater microstructural stability over time compared to the untreated (undoped) baseline.
generation.baseline: Performance observed in standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy bond coats without Y and Hf intervention.
generation.boundary: The improved performance is expected to hold under high-temperature conditions (~900 °C) and in the specified molten salt environment; its efficacy at significantly higher temperatures or in drastically different corrosive environments has not been established.
generation.uncertainty: While existing evidence (PMC10488378::page::002) supports the potential benefits of Y and Hf co-doping in terms of oxidation resistance and microstructural stability, the long-term durability under cyclic thermal loads and extended exposure times remains to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of bond coat samples: one using standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and the other co-doped with Y and Hf during laser cladding. Subject both groups to prolonged exposure at 900 °C in a molten salt mixture (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) and simulate thermal cycling representative of service conditions.
measurements: Oxide scale growth rate and composition
Microstructural analysis (phase stability and distribution via SEM/TEM and XRD)
Hot corrosion rate determination (mass change measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the co-doped samples do not display statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance, microstructural integrity, and hot corrosion performance compared to the undoped controls, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: tings. In the HEA system, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with a BCC+FCC eutectic microstructure was first proposed by Lu in 2014 []. Here, the eutectic structure offers enhanced strength, hardness, toughness, and corrosion resistance. Therefore, EHEA has a wider range of potential applications compared to traditional alloys [,]. Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,].
